# Laos TRAVEL SURVIVAL KIT **Last Updated**: October 26, 2023 **Traveler Types Covered**: Budget/Luxury/Family/Solo/Backpacker ## 1. SIM CARD SOLUTIONS **Purpose**: Obtain local mobile connectivity for calls, data, and internet access. #### Key Information to Research | **Aspect** | **Details to Find** | |:---|:---| | **Providers** | Unitel, Lao Telecom, ETL | | **Price Options** | **Unitel:** 7-day (10,000-20,000 LAK for 3-5GB), 15-day (25,000-40,000 LAK for 6-10GB), 30-day (50,000-100,000 LAK for 15-30GB+). Prices vary seasonally and with promotions.
**Lao Telecom:** Similar packages, often slightly higher price point or lower data.
**ETL:** Generally cheapest, but less reliable coverage outside major cities. | | **Data Allocation** | Most tourist plans offer high-speed data (e.g., 3GB, 5GB, 10GB, 20GB) with unlimited data at reduced speeds thereafter. Specific limits depend on the package. | | **Validity Period** | Typically 7, 15, or 30 days. Longer-term plans (60/90 days) also available for extended stays. | | **Hotspot/Tethering** | Generally allowed on all major networks. | | **Coverage** | **Unitel:** Widest and most reliable coverage, especially strong in rural areas and between major cities.
**Lao Telecom:** Excellent in cities and major towns, good along main transport routes.
**ETL:** Good in Vientiane and Luang Prabang, weaker elsewhere. | | **Where to Buy** | **Airports:** Wattay International Airport (Vientiane), Luang Prabang International Airport. Look for official kiosks after immigration/baggage claim.
**Convenience Stores:** Limited options, mostly top-ups.
**Official Shops:** Dedicated branches in major towns (Vientiane, Luang Prabang, Pakse) offer full registration and support. You'll need your passport. | | **Alternative: eSIM** | **Airalo:** (e.g., Discover Global, AsiaLink) offers regional and global plans, 1GB for 7 days (~$5 USD), 3GB for 30 days (~$11 USD).
**Holafly:** Unlimited data plans for Laos, starting from 5 days (~$19 USD) to 30 days (~$44 USD).
**Other providers:** MobiMatter, Nomad. | #### Recommendations Framework - **Short trips (3-5 days) + visiting neighboring countries?** → **Airalo/Holafly eSIM** for ease of activation and multi-country options, or a **Unitel physical SIM from the airport** if staying only in Laos. - **Staying 1-4 weeks?** → A **Unitel 15-day or 30-day physical SIM** bought at the airport or an official store will provide the best balance of coverage and data. - **Digital nomad preferences?** → **eSIM** for convenience and flexibility, especially if hopping between countries. Unitel's physical SIM is a strong backup for reliable local coverage. - **Budget-conscious?** → **ETL** offers the lowest prices but be aware of potentially spottier coverage. Unitel often has competitive promotions. Compare per-GB cost at the airport kiosks. ## 2. AIRPORT TRANSFERS **Purpose**: Navigate from main airport to nearest major city center efficiently. **Route**: From Wattay International Airport (VTE) to Vientiane City Center (approx. 5-7 km) **Route**: From Luang Prabang International Airport (LPQ) to Luang Prabang City Center (approx. 4-5 km) #### Key Information to Research | **Mode** | **Duration** | **Cost (LAK/USD)** | **Booking** | **Convenience** | **Best For** | |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| | **VTE - Vientiane City Center** | | | | | | | **Airport Taxi (Fixed Fare)** | 15-25 min | 50,000-70,000 LAK (~$3-4 USD) | Airport counter | Very Good | Door-to-door, any time, luggage | | **LOCA (Ride-hailing App)** | 15-25 min | 35,000-60,000 LAK (~$2-3.5 USD) | App-based | Excellent | Budget-conscious, clear pricing, late night | | **Tuk-tuk** | 20-30 min | 30,000-50,000 LAK (~$1.8-3 USD) | Negotiate at exit | Good | Budget, short distances, local experience | | **Airport Bus** | Currently very limited/unreliable/non-existent. Not recommended. | N/A | N/A | Poor | N/A | | **Hotel Shuttle** | Varies | 50,000-100,000 LAK (~$3-6 USD) | Contact hotel | Very Good | Convenience, pre-arranged, high-end hotels | | **LPQ - Luang Prabang City Center** | | | | | | | **Shared Minivan/Shuttle** | 15-20 min | 50,000 LAK (~$3 USD) per person | Airport counter | Excellent | Budget, solo/couples, efficient | | **Private Taxi** | 15-20 min | 70,000-90,000 LAK (~$4-5 USD) | Airport counter | Very Good | Door-to-door, groups, luggage | | **Tuk-tuk** | 20-25 min | 40,000-60,000 LAK (~$2.5-3.5 USD) | Negotiate at exit | Good | Budget, local experience, short distances | #### Detail Each Option With **Vientiane - Wattay International Airport (VTE) to City Center** * **Airport Taxi (Fixed Fare)** * **Exact boarding location**: Official taxi counter inside the arrival hall, just past baggage claim. Pay at the counter, then proceed to the designated taxi queue outside. * **Frequency**: Available continuously during airport operating hours (approx. 6 AM - 10 PM), less frequent late at night but usually still possible. * **Final drop-off location**: Your specific hotel or guesthouse in the city center. * **How to purchase tickets**: Purchase a voucher at the official counter. * **Operating hours**: Aligns with flight schedules. * **Time estimates**: 15-25 minutes, minimal traffic impact in Vientiane. * **LOCA (Ride-hailing App)** * **Exact boarding location**: Order via the app upon arrival. Drivers will usually meet at the main pickup/drop-off area outside the terminal. * **Frequency**: On-demand, typically 5-10 minute wait times. * **Final drop-off location**: Your specific hotel or guesthouse. * **How to purchase tickets**: Book and pay (cash or card) via the app. * **Operating hours**: 24/7, though fewer drivers late at night. * **Time estimates**: 15-25 minutes. * **Tuk-tuk** * **Exact boarding location**: Walk out of the terminal past the official taxi stand. Tuk-tuk drivers will approach you. * **Frequency**: Abundant during the day, less reliable very late at night. * **Final drop-off location**: Your specific hotel or guesthouse. * **How to purchase tickets**: Negotiate price directly with the driver before boarding. * **Operating hours**: Daytime until late evening. * **Time estimates**: 20-30 minutes. **Luang Prabang - Luang Prabang International Airport (LPQ) to City Center** * **Shared Minivan/Shuttle** * **Exact boarding location**: Buy a ticket at the "Minivan" or "Shuttle" counter inside the arrival hall. Minivans depart from just outside the terminal. * **Frequency**: Minivans wait to fill up, or depart every 15-30 minutes, especially after flight arrivals. * **Final drop-off location**: They drop passengers directly at their hotels/guesthouses in the city center. * **How to purchase tickets**: Purchase a ticket at the designated counter. * **Operating hours**: Aligns with flight schedules, typically 7 AM - 9 PM. * **Time estimates**: 15-20 minutes depending on other drop-offs. * **Private Taxi** * **Exact boarding location**: Taxi counter inside the arrival hall. * **Frequency**: Available continuously during airport operating hours. * **Final drop-off location**: Your specific hotel or guesthouse. * **How to purchase tickets**: Purchase a voucher at the official counter. * **Operating hours**: Aligns with flight schedules. * **Time estimates**: 15-20 minutes. * **Tuk-tuk** * **Exact boarding location**: Walk out of the terminal. Drivers will be waiting. * **Frequency**: Abundant during the day, less reliable very late at night. * **Final drop-off location**: Your specific hotel or guesthouse. * **How to purchase tickets**: Negotiate price directly with the driver before boarding. * **Operating hours**: Daytime until late evening. * **Time estimates**: 20-25 minutes. ## 3. CURRENCY EXCHANGE **Purpose**: Convert home currency to local currency at best rates. **Current Exchange Rate**: 1 USD ≈ 19,000 – 21,000 LAK (Lao Kip) (as of Oct 2023, highly variable due to inflation) **Note:** While USD and Thai Baht (THB) are widely accepted in tourist areas and for larger purchases, using Lao Kip (LAK) for smaller transactions and everyday items generally offers better value. #### Best Exchange Locations | **Location** | **Why It's Best** | **Address / Area** | **Hours** | **Rates** | **Tips** | |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| | **BCEL Bank / BFL Bank** | Government-owned/private banks, reliable & transparent rates | Major branches in Vientiane (e.g., Fa Ngum Rd, Lane Xang Ave) & Luang Prabang (e.g., Sisavangvong Rd) | Mon-Fri, 8:30 AM - 3:30 PM | Generally good, official rates | Bring passport; expect queues. | | **Licensed Money Changers** | Often slightly better rates than banks, faster service | Vientiane: Near Talat Sao (Morning Market), Fa Ngum Road. Luang Prabang: Main street (Sisavangvong Road). | Varies, usually 8 AM - 6 PM | Can be very competitive; compare a few. | Check for official signage and license before exchanging. | | **Gold Shops** | Surprisingly good rates in some areas | Vientiane: Talat Sao area. Luang Prabang: Night Market side streets. | Varies, usually 9 AM - 7 PM | Often competitive, but verify before. | Use trusted, established gold shops; always double-check the amount. | #### Alternative Methods | **Method** | **Pros** | **Cons** | **Best For** | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | **ATM Withdrawal** | Convenient, access to LAK directly, generally decent rates | High fees (both local bank fee ~20,000-30,000 LAK per transaction, plus your home bank's fees), withdrawal limits (1,000,000-2,000,000 LAK per transaction) | Quick cash, when banks are closed, reliable source | | **Airport Exchange** | Immediate access, convenient upon arrival | Higher margins, worse rates (10-15% less than city) | Emergency small amounts only for initial transport/SIM | | **Credit Card** | Secure, good for tracking expenses, mid-market rates | Foreign transaction fees (check your card), not accepted everywhere (especially street stalls, small shops), occasional surcharges (3-5%) | Large purchases (hotels, upscale restaurants, tour agencies) | | **Bank Transfer (e.g., Wise/Revolut)** | Best rates if pre-arranged, lower fees than traditional banks | Time-consuming, requires local bank account (not for tourists), usually not practical for short trips | Long-term stays, digital nomads | #### Universal Tips - Avoid exchanging at the airport unless for small emergency cash. - Always compare rates between 2-3 money changers/banks before committing. - Carry cash in smaller denominations (10,000 LAK, 20,000 LAK) for markets and tuk-tuks. Large notes are difficult to break. - Check for hidden commissions or fees before exchanging. Laos generally has transparent exchanges. - Best time to exchange: during banking hours for best rates and security. - Have small cash (USD/THB) on arrival for initial expenses if you don't want to use airport exchange. ## 4. MUST-HAVE APPS **Purpose**: Essential applications for navigation, transport, payments, and communication. #### Category: Transportation | **App** | **Purpose** | **Key Features** | |:---|:---|:---| | **LOCA** | Ride-hailing (Car, Tuk-tuk) | Upfront pricing, driver tracking, cash/card payments, airport transfers | | **Google Maps** | Navigation & Public Transport | Real-time traffic, offline maps, directions for walking/driving/public transport (limited for Lao public transport outside Vientiane) | | **12Go.Asia** | Bus/Train/Ferry Booking | Online booking for intercity buses, trains (Vientiane-Luang Prabang high-speed rail), ferries; reliable for checking schedules. | #### Category: Payments & Wallet | **App** | **Purpose** | **Key Features** | |:---|:---|:---| | **Unitel Money / M-Money (Lao Telecom)** | Local mobile wallets | Cashless payments, peer-to-peer transfers, bill payments (primarily for locals) | | **QR Pay (BFL Bank App)** | QR code payments | Accepted at some modern businesses for quick payments. | #### Category: Food & Delivery | **App** | **Purpose** | **Key Features** | |:---|:---|:---| | **Foodpanda** | Food, grocery & essential delivery | Restaurant variety, real-time tracking, convenient for hotels/guesthouses in Vientiane & Luang Prabang | #### Category: Information & Entertainment | **App** | **Purpose** | **Key Features** | |:---|:---|:---| | **AccuWeather / Google Weather** | Local weather | Accurate forecasts, rain alerts (crucial during rainy season) | | **TripAdvisor / Google Reviews** | Local Restaurants & Attractions | User reviews, photos, operating hours, contact info for establishments | | **Facebook / Instagram** | Local Happenings & Discoveries | Many local businesses, cafes, and event organizers use these platforms for announcements and promotions. | ## 5. MUST-TRY FOODS **Purpose**: Experience authentic local cuisine and signature dishes. 🍽️ **Larb (ລາບ)** – Minced Meat Salad → **What**: Laos' national dish. A spicy and sour minced meat salad (chicken, beef, pork, or fish) mixed with ground toasted rice, lime juice, fish sauce, herbs (mint, coriander, spring onion), and chili. → **Why it's famous**: Its vibrant flavor profile, freshness, and cultural significance. It embodies the Lao love for bold, aromatic spices. → **Flavor profile**: Zesty, savory, herbaceous, with a spicy kick and a subtle nutty crunch from the toasted rice. → **Best location**: Almost any local restaurant in Vientiane or Luang Prabang (e.g., 'Kop Chai Deu' in Vientiane, 'Coconut Garden' in Luang Prabang). Also readily available at street food stalls. → **Average price**: 30,000 - 60,000 LAK (~$1.5-3 USD) → **Pro tip**: Always eaten with sticky rice (Khao Niaw). Wrap a small ball of sticky rice in your hand and use it to scoop up the Larb. 🍽️ **Tam Mak Hoong (ຕໍາໝາກຫຸ່ງ)** – Green Papaya Salad → **What**: Similar to Thai Som Tum but often more pungent and sour with fermented fish sauce (padek). Shredded green papaya pounded with garlic, chili, tomatoes, long beans, lime, sugar, and padek. → **Why it's famous**: Its intense, complex flavors and the interactive pounding preparation method. A staple in Lao diets. → **Flavor profile**: Spicy, sour, salty, savory, with a strong umami kick from the padek. → **Best location**: Street food stalls and local markets (e.g., Vientiane Night Market, Luang Prabang Morning Market). Many local restaurants also serve it. → **Average price**: 20,000 - 40,000 LAK (~$1-2 USD) → **Pro tip**: Specify your preferred spice level ("bo phet" for no chili, "phet noi" for a little, "phet lai" for very spicy). Pair with sticky rice and grilled meat. 🍽️ **Khao Piak Sen (ເຂົ້າປຽກເສັ້ນ)** – Lao Noodle Soup → **What**: A comforting and hearty noodle soup with thick, hand-cut rice noodles in a rich pork or chicken broth. Often topped with sliced chicken or pork, meatballs, fried garlic, and fresh herbs. → **Why it's famous**: A quintessential Lao comfort food, especially popular for breakfast or a late-night snack. → **Flavor profile**: Savory, deeply umami, with a slightly chewy texture from the fresh noodles. Often customized with chili oil, lime, and fish sauce. → **Best location**: Small local eateries and street food stalls specializing in noodles (look for signs saying "Khao Piak"). → **Average price**: 20,000 - 35,000 LAK (~$1-1.8 USD) → **Pro tip**: Add a squeeze of lime, a dash of fish sauce, and a spoonful of chili flakes to taste. Often served with a side of patongko (fried dough sticks) for dipping. 🍽️ **Sien Savanh (ຊີ້ນສະຫວັນ)** – Lao Dried Beef → **What**: Thin strips of marinated beef, sun-dried and then lightly fried or grilled until tender and chewy. Marinated with garlic, ginger, sesame seeds, and soy sauce. → **Why it's famous**: A popular snack or appetizer, perfect with sticky rice or a cold Beerlao. → **Flavor profile**: Sweet, savory, garlicky, with a smoky aroma and a satisfying chewiness. → **Best location**: Appetizer at many restaurants, or sold pre-packaged at markets (e.g., Morning Market in Vientiane) or roadside stalls. → **Average price**: 30,000 - 50,000 LAK (~$1.5-2.5 USD) for a small plate. → **Pro tip**: Excellent beer snack. Some variations use buffalo meat (Sien Kwai Savanh), which is even more tender. 🍽️ **Mok Pa (ໝົກປາ)** – Steamed Fish in Banana Leaf → **What**: Freshwater fish (often Tilapia or Mekong river fish) marinated in a rich paste of lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, chili, garlic, fish sauce, and dill, then steamed in a banana leaf packet. → **Why it's famous**: A healthy, flavorful, and aromatic dish that showcases traditional Lao cooking methods. → **Flavor profile**: Aromatic, herbal, savory, with a delicate fish flavor and a mild spicy kick. → **Best location**: Mid-range to upscale Lao restaurants (e.g., 'Khop Chai Deu' in Vientiane, 'Manda de Laos' in Luang Prabang). → **Average price**: 50,000 - 80,000 LAK (~$2.5-4 USD) → **Pro tip**: Unfold the banana leaf at the table to release the fragrant steam. Eat with sticky rice. 🍽️ **Khao Niaw (ເຂົ້າໜຽວ)** – Sticky Rice → **What**: Glutinous rice, typically steamed in a bamboo basket. The staple food of Laos, eaten with almost every meal. → **Why it's famous**: Central to Lao cuisine and culture. It's often said that Laotians eat more sticky rice per capita than any other country. → **Flavor profile**: Mildly sweet, chewy, and slightly firm. → **Best location**: Served with almost every savory dish in Laos, from street stalls to fine dining. → **Average price**: 5,000 - 10,000 LAK (~$0.25-0.5 USD) for a basket. → **Pro tip**: Use your right hand to form small, bite-sized balls of sticky rice to accompany other dishes. 🍽️ **Beerlao (ເບຍລາວ)** – Local Lager → **What**: Laos's highly popular national beer, a light and crisp lager brewed with rice and malt. → **Why it's famous**: Consistently ranked among the best beers in Southeast Asia, almost a national symbol. → **Flavor profile**: Refreshing, smooth, slightly malty with a clean finish. → **Best location**: Universally available in supermarkets, convenience stores, restaurants, and bars across Laos. → **Average price**: 10,000 - 20,000 LAK (~$0.5-1 USD) for a large bottle in a shop; 15,000 - 30,000 LAK (~$0.8-1.5 USD) in a restaurant/bar. → **Pro tip**: Enjoy ice-cold, often served with a glass of ice. Also try Beerlao Dark Lager for a richer, sweeter taste. ## 6. Often infused with herbs or snakes (for medicinal purposes, though controversial). | **Local markets:** Often sold in plastic bottles. **Specialty liquor stores.** **Some tourist shops (small decorative bottles).** | 50,000 - 200,000 LAK (~$2.5-10 USD) for a bottle, depending on size/quality. | For bottled liquor, pack securely in checked luggage. Be mindful of liquid limits and customs rules. Avoid snake-infused variants for ethical reasons and import restrictions. | ## 7. SUPERMARKETS & CONVENIENCE STORES **Purpose**: Access everyday items, snacks, and groceries reliably. **Major Cities**: Vientiane, Luang Prabang, Pakse **Major Supermarket Chains** * **V-Mart / M-Point Mart** * **Type**: Mid-size Supermarket / Convenience Store hybrid * **Coverage**: Good presence in Vientiane and Luang Prabang, with multiple branches. * **Best for**: General groceries, snacks, beverages (including alcohol), toiletries, basic household items. Good selection of Beerlao and local snacks. * **Price level**: Mid-range. * **Specialty**: Often open later than traditional markets, reliable for quick buys. * **Hours**: Typically 8 AM - 9 PM. * **Locations**: Vientiane: Dongpalane Road, Khouvieng Road. Luang Prabang: Along Sisavangvong Road and nearby streets. * **J-Mart** * **Type**: Smaller Supermarket / Convenience Store * **Coverage**: Primarily Vientiane, with a few branches. * **Best for**: Daily essentials, fresh produce (limited), snacks, drinks. * **Price level**: Budget to Mid-range. * **Specialty**: Often found in residential areas, good for local prices. * **Hours**: Varies, typically 7 AM - 9 PM. * **Locations**: Vientiane: Various neighborhoods. **Convenience Stores** * **Minimart (Local Shops)** * **Type**: Local Convenience Store * **Coverage**: Ubiquitous throughout all towns and cities. * **Best for**: Cold drinks, snacks, instant noodles, basic toiletries, cigarettes, Beerlao. * **Price level**: Budget. * **Specialty**: Open long hours, some 24/7. Very convenient for quick needs. * **Hours**: Many are 24/7, others 6 AM - 10 PM. * **Locations**: Every street corner in tourist areas and residential zones. **Pharmacy Chains** * **Local Pharmacies** * **Type**: Pharmacy * **Coverage**: Numerous independent pharmacies in every town. * **Best for**: Over-the-counter medication, basic first-aid supplies, some cosmetics, common antibiotics (often available without prescription). * **Price level**: Budget to Mid-range. * **Specialty**: Look for "Pharmacy" or "ຮ້ານຂາຍຢາ" signs. English-speaking pharmacists are rare outside major tourist areas. * **Hours**: Typically 8 AM - 8 PM. * **Locations**: Main streets in Vientiane (e.g., Rue Setthathirath), Luang Prabang (Sisavangvong Road). **Department Store Supermarkets (Upscale Options)** * **Talat Sao Mall Supermarket (Vientiane)** * **Type**: Department Store Supermarket * **Coverage**: One main location within Talat Sao Mall. * **Best for**: Wider selection of imported goods, fresh produce, meat, dairy, cosmetics, electronics. Air-conditioned comfort. * **Price level**: Premium for imported goods, mid-range for local. * **Specialty**: Modern shopping experience, good for serious grocery runs. * **Hours**: 9 AM - 9 PM. * **Locations**: Inside Talat Sao Mall, Vientiane. **Key Details Per Store** - **Selection variety**: Generally good for local essentials; imported goods are more expensive and limited. - **Price competitiveness**: Local minimarts and wet markets offer the best prices for fresh produce. Supermarkets are convenient but slightly pricier. - **English signage availability**: Generally good in tourist areas for major chains; limited in local shops. - **Payment methods accepted**: Cash (LAK) is king. Credit cards accepted at larger supermarkets and some M-Point Marts, but expect a surcharge (2-3%). - **Closest location to tourist areas**: Minimarts are everywhere. For larger supermarkets, look up specific addresses on Google Maps. In Luang Prabang, M-Point Marts are conveniently located on the main road. ## 8. Bargain politely (10-30% off). | | **Vientiane Night Market (Riverside)** | Along the Mekong River promenade, near Chao Anouvong Park | Daily, 6 PM - 10 PM | Clothing, accessories, electronics, local snacks, street food | More focused on local consumer goods and fashion than tourist souvenirs. Food stalls along the river. | Come for the atmosphere and river views. Eat at the food stalls, but don't expect extensive souvenir shopping. | | **Pakse Night Market** | Along the Mekong River, near the Pakse Bridge | Daily, 5 PM - 10 PM | Local food, drinks, clothing, small electronics | Authentic local experience with fewer tourists. Excellent variety of Laotian street food and cheap Beerlao. | Great for an authentic local meal and to observe local life. Very friendly atmosphere. | #### Day Markets | **Market Name** | **Location** | **Open Hours** | **Best For** | **What to Expect** | **Pro Tips** | |:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---| | **Talat Sao (Morning Market), Vientiane** | Corner of Lane Xang Ave and Kouvieng Rd, Vientiane | Daily, 7 AM - 5 PM (some stalls earlier/later) | Textiles, jewelry, electronics, local products, gold shops | A large complex with an indoor mall (air-conditioned) and outdoor market stalls. Wide range of goods from traditional Lao items to modern electronics. | Go early for fresh produce in the outdoor section. Indoor mall is good for escaping the heat and finding specific items. | | **Luang Prabang Morning Market** | Sakkaline Road (behind the Royal Palace Museum) | Daily, 6 AM - 11 AM | Fresh produce, local snacks, cooked food, meat, fish | A bustling, authentic local wet market. Watch monks collect alms. Raw ingredients and ready-to-eat Lao breakfast items. | Visit very early (before 7 AM) to see alms-giving. Be respectful and do not interfere. Excellent for photo opportunities. | #### Specialty Markets - **Wet Markets**: Both Talat Sao and Luang Prabang Morning Market have extensive wet market sections for fresh produce, meat, and seafood. A fascinating cultural experience, but can be pungent and muddy. - **Craft Markets**: Luang Prabang Night Market is the primary craft market. Ock Pop Tok (Luang Prabang) offers a more curated, fair-trade craft experience. - **Antique Markets**: Limited, but some stalls within Talat Sao or specialized shops in Luang Prabang may sell vintage items or "antiques" (verify authenticity carefully). - **Fashion Markets**: Talat Sao (indoor mall) and Vientiane Night Market are best for local fashion, particularly casual clothing and accessories. #### Universal Night/Day Market Tips - Carry cash (small denominations like 10,000 LAK, 20,000 LAK, 50,000 LAK are ideal). - Most stalls don't accept cards. - Visit early (for day markets) or at dusk (for night markets) to beat crowds and enjoy the ambiance. - Bargaining is expected in most Lao markets, especially for souvenirs and clothing. Start at 50% of the asking price and aim for 20-30% off. Do so politely and with a smile. - Street food is freshest when stalls are busy and turnover is high. Look for stalls popular with locals. - Best for photography and atmosphere at sunset (night markets) and early morning (morning markets). Always ask before photographing people. ## 9. LOCAL FESTIVALS & EVENTS (Optional) - **Pi Mai Lao (Lao New Year)**: Mid-April (usually April 13-15). * **Cultural significance**: The most important festival, marked by water splashing, temple visits, and family gatherings to cleanse for the new year. * **Where to celebrate**: Celebrated nationwide, with the biggest and most vibrant celebrations in Luang Prabang and Vientiane. * **Booking requirements**: Book accommodation and transport well in advance (6+ months) as it's peak season. * **Crowd management tips**: Embrace the water fights but protect electronics. Dress lightly. - **Boun That Luang (That Luang Festival)**: Full moon of the 12th lunar month (usually November). * **Cultural significance**: Most important Buddhist festival in Laos, centering around the Pha That Luang stupa in Vientiane. Involves religious ceremonies, parades, music, and a large fair. * **Where to celebrate**: Pha That Luang, Vientiane. * **Booking requirements**: Accommodation in Vientiane should be booked in advance. * **Crowd management tips**: Expect large crowds, especially around the stupa. Dress respectfully (shoulders and knees covered). - **Boun Ok Phansa (End of Buddhist Lent)**: Full moon of the 11th lunar month (usually October). * **Cultural significance**: Marks the end of the rainy season and Buddhist Lent. Celebrated with boat races (especially in Vientiane on the Mekong) and illuminated boat processions (Lai Heua Fai) where offerings are floated down rivers. * **Where to celebrate**: Vientiane (boat races), Luang Prabang (Lai Heua Fai). * **Booking requirements**: Accommodation might be tighter in Vientiane during the boat race. * **Crowd management tips**: Find a spot along the Mekong River for the boat races or illuminated boats. ## 12. LOCAL CUSTOMS & ETIQUETTE A thorough etiquette section is non-negotiable in any Travel Survival Kit. Cultural missteps — even unintentional ones — can cause offence, deny entry to sacred sites, or make interactions unnecessarily difficult. #### 12a. Temple & Sacred Site Dress Code Dress codes at religious and heritage sites are strictly enforced worldwide — research and communicate the exact rules for the destination. | **Rule** | **What to Check** | **Enforcement Level** | |:---|:---|:---| | **Shoulders covered** | Sleeveless tops / tank tops prohibited | Very strict at most temples and sacred sites (e.g., That Luang, Wat Xieng Thong). | | **Knees covered** | Shorts / mini-skirts prohibited | Strictly enforced at major temples. | | **Footwear** | Shoes removed before entry | Mandatory when entering the main chapel (sim) of a temple or any private home. | | **Head covering** | Not typically required for women at Buddhist temples. | Not applicable for most Buddhist temples. | | **Colour restrictions** | None specific, but modest colours are always respectful. Avoid overly flamboyant clothing. | None specific. | | **Sarong/Wrap rental** | Not as common as in Cambodia/Thailand. Best to arrive dressed appropriately. | Unreliable. | > **Laos-specific rules:** > - **Shoulders AND knees must be covered** at all temples and sacred sites. This includes Pha That Luang in Vientiane, Wat Xieng Thong in Luang Prabang, and other important religious locations. Guards or temple officials will check and may deny entry or require you to purchase a suitable covering. > - **Lightweight linen trousers or long skirts and a modest t-shirt** or blouse are ideal in the heat. Avoid sleeveless shirts, short shorts, and anything revealing entirely. > - **Shoes must always be removed** when entering the *sim* (ordination hall or main prayer area) of a temple, or when entering a local home. Look for a pile of shoes outside the entrance as a cue. > **Pro format tip:** Always state: *"T-shirts and lightweight long pants or long skirts are the perfect temple outfit — simple, cool, and always accepted."* Give travelers the positive solution, not just the list of prohibitions. #### 12b. The Head, Feet & Body — Cultural Hierarchy Many Asian and South/Southeast Asian cultures observe a strict spiritual hierarchy of the human body. Get this wrong and the offence is serious. **Universal rules to research per destination:** - **The head is sacred**: Never touch another person on the head — not adults, not children. This applies in Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and much of South and Southeast Asia. The head is considered the highest and most spiritual part of the body. - **The feet are considered the lowest and most impure part of the body**: Never point the soles of your feet at a person, a Buddha statue, a shrine, or a religious image. When sitting on the floor in a temple or a local home, tuck feet away from sacred objects and other people. Avoid stepping over people or food. - **Passing objects**: Use your right hand (or both hands) when giving or receiving items, especially money or important documents. The left hand is traditionally considered unclean. > **Laos-specific:** > - Never touch a Laotian person's head — even a child's. This is a significant cultural violation regardless of how affectionately it is intended. > - When seated near Buddha statues or monks, ensure the soles of your feet point away. Reclining with feet pointed toward the altar is deeply disrespectful. Always point your feet away from people and sacred objects. #### 12c. Monk Interactions & Religious Etiquette Monks are afforded the highest social respect in Buddhist countries. Specific rules apply that are not obvious to foreign visitors. | **Rule** | **Detail** | **Who It Applies To** | |:---|:---|:---| | **Women cannot touch monks** | No physical contact under any circumstances. This includes brushing past, handing items directly, or sitting too close. | All women | | **Women handing items to monks** | Must place the item on a surface or table, or hand it to a male intermediary — never hand it directly. | All women | | **Men offering items** | Can be handed directly, but use both hands respectfully. | All men | | **Photography of monks** | Always ask permission first — many monks are comfortable, some are not. Avoid flash photography during alms-giving. | All visitors | | **Entering monastery grounds** | Dress code applies — same as temple rules (shoulders/knees covered). | All visitors | | **Morning alms-giving (Tak Bat)** | Observe silently and respectfully from a distance. Do not interrupt the procession, use flash photography, or try to get too close. If participating, purchase appropriate food offerings beforehand and dress respectfully. | All visitors | > **Laos-specific:** Women must never touch a monk or hand anything directly to one. If a woman needs to give something to a monk, she should place it on a nearby table or surface and allow the monk to pick it up. During the alms-giving ceremony in Luang Prabang, maintain a respectful distance, avoid talking loudly, and do not use flash photography. Do not try to participate unless you are fully prepared and dressed appropriately, and are doing so out of genuine respect rather than as a photo opportunity. #### 12d. Saving Face & Conflict Resolution "Saving face" is a central social concept across most of East, Southeast, and South Asia. Public embarrassment — for either party — is to be avoided at all costs. **Key rules:** - **Never raise your voice, shout, or show visible anger in public** — regardless of how frustrated you are. A calm demeanour is always more effective and earns respect. - **Smile through difficult negotiations** — in Laos, a genuine smile is the most powerful negotiating tool a visitor has. This applies in markets, with tuk-tuk drivers, and in guesthouses. - **Public confrontations always backfire** — if a vendor, driver, or official makes an error, address it quietly and privately. A public accusation humiliates the other person and ends any chance of resolution. - **"Yes" does not always mean yes** — in many Asian cultures, saying "no" directly is considered impolite. A vague answer, a smile, or a change of subject may mean "no." Read context carefully. Patience is key. - **Patience is a virtue with practical value** — losing patience visibly signals weakness and often results in worse outcomes. Those who remain calm, polite, and persistent are far more successful. > **Laos-specific:** Showing anger or creating a public scene is deeply embarrassing for both parties and will not get you what you want. Always maintain a calm, smiling demeanor when negotiating or resolving issues — in markets, with drivers, and especially with any officials. Laos operates at a slower pace; embrace "Lao time" and avoid becoming visibly frustrated by delays. #### 12e. Responsible Tourism & Child Welfare This section is especially important in developing-country destinations and must be included prominently. **Core principles:** - **Do not give money, candy, or gifts to begging children at temples or tourist sites.** This directly incentivises parents and local networks to keep children out of school and working the tourist circuit instead. The kindness feels real but causes lasting harm. - **Support legitimate alternatives instead:** - Eat at NGO-run training restaurants (in Luang Prabang: Tamarind Restaurant sometimes offers training, or look for specific social enterprises). - Buy crafts from certified fair-trade cooperatives (e.g., Ock Pop Tok in Luang Prabang). - Donate to verified local organisations rather than individuals on the street. - **Orphanage tourism is harmful:** Many "orphanages" in developing countries are not genuine — children are recruited from living families to attract tourist donations. Do not visit or donate to orphanages in Laos. - **Animal welfare:** Do not ride elephants (harmful), visit venues with performing wildlife, or pay for photos with captive animals. Support ethical elephant sanctuaries where direct interaction is limited and the focus is on rehabilitation. - **Ask before photographing people** — especially children, monks, and market vendors. A smile and a gesture asking permission takes two seconds and is always the right choice. **Where to direct travelers for legitimate giving:** - **Big Brother Mouse (Luang Prabang):** A non-profit that produces children's books and fosters literacy. Tourists can participate in "English practice" sessions with local students. - **Ock Pop Tok (Luang Prabang):** A traditional Lao textile and craft center committed to fair trade, preserving traditional skills, and empowering women. - **Free The Bears Laos (Luang Prabang):** Supports the protection and rehabilitation of sun and moon bears. - **Verify organisations:** Look for local NGOs with clear missions and transparent financial reporting if you wish to donate directly. #### 12f. General Social Customs & Greetings Cover the standard social customs relevant to the destination: - **Greeting style**: The "Nop" (similar to the Thai Wai) is the traditional greeting. Place your palms together in a prayer-like gesture at chest level and bow slightly. The higher the hands (up to the nose), the more respect shown. Generally, a younger person will Nop an older person first, and the older person will return a lower Nop. A simple "Sabaidee" (hello) is also polite. - **Tipping culture**: Tipping is not mandatory or traditionally expected in Laos. However, in tourist-oriented restaurants, hotels, and for good service from guides or drivers, a small tip (rounding up the bill, 10-20,000 LAK) is appreciated. - **Dress outside temples**: While less strict than in temples, modesty is generally appreciated in Laos. Avoid excessively revealing clothing, especially in rural areas or when visiting local villages. In cities like Vientiane and Luang Prabang, casual Western wear is common, but respect local sensibilities. - **Photography restrictions**: Generally, photography is allowed, but always ask permission before photographing people, especially monks or ethnic minorities. Photography is prohibited in some government buildings, military sites, and specific areas within museums or temples. Respect "no photography" signs. - **Public displays of affection**: Public displays of affection (kissing, excessive hugging) are generally frowned upon and considered inappropriate in Laos. Hold hands if you wish, but keep it modest. - **Bargaining norms**: Bargaining is expected and common in markets (day and night markets) for souvenirs, clothing, and sometimes tuk-tuk fares. It is generally not done in shops with fixed prices (supermarkets, convenience stores, modern restaurants). Always bargain politely and with a smile. - **Dining etiquette**: Sticky rice is eaten with your right hand. Food is often served family-style, with dishes shared. Do not point your feet at food or other diners. It's polite to wait for elders or hosts to start eating. Slurping noodles is acceptable. ## 13. SAFETY & PRACTICAL INFORMATION Safety and health information must be specific, actionable, and honest. Vague reassurances ("generally safe") are not useful. Give travelers real data and real guidance. #### 13a. Vaccinations & Preventative Health Always verify current WHO and destination-country health recommendations. The following framework applies to most tropical and developing-country destinations. **Vaccination research checklist:** | **Vaccine / Medication** | **Priority Level** | **Notes** | |:---|:---|:---| | **Hepatitis A** | Strongly recommended | Transmitted through contaminated food/water — essential for any developing country like Laos. | | **Hepatitis B** | Recommended | Especially for longer stays (over a month), or those anticipating medical/dental procedures or close contact with locals. | | **Typhoid** | Recommended | High risk in areas with poor sanitation and street food consumption, common throughout Laos. | | **Tetanus / Diphtheria (Td/Tdap)** | Recommended | Ensure booster is current (within 10 years). Important due to risk of injury. | | **Japanese Encephalitis** | Destination-specific | Recommended for rural/agricultural areas and longer stays (over 3-4 weeks) in Southeast Asia, especially during the rainy season. | | **Rabies pre-exposure** | Destination-specific | Recommended for adventurous travel, those working with animals, or prolonged stays in rural areas where access to post-exposure treatment might be limited. Laos has rabies risk. | | **Malaria prophylaxis** | Destination-specific | Generally NOT needed for major tourist hubs and cities like Vientiane and Luang Prabang. Required for some rural/border regions (e.g., southern Laos, border areas with Cambodia/Myanmar). Consult a travel doctor. | | **Cholera** | Destination-specific | Generally not required for most tourists unless visiting high-risk flood/disaster zones. | > **Laos-specific:** Hepatitis A, Typhoid, and Tetanus are recommended for all visitors. Malaria prophylaxis is generally NOT required for Vientiane, Luang Prabang, and main tourist corridors — consult a travel doctor for rural/border regions (e.g., southern Laos, areas near Cambodia/Myanmar borders, northern Laos). Always bring DEET-based insect repellent regardless of malaria risk, due to dengue. **Always advise travelers to:** - Consult a travel medicine clinic or GP 6-8 weeks before departure to discuss specific vaccination needs based on their itinerary, duration, and personal health. - Carry a small first-aid kit (antihistamine, rehydration sachets, antiseptic wipes, blister plasters, diarrhoea medication like Imodium/Loperamide, pain relievers). - Know their travel insurance emergency evacuation coverage and keep the emergency contact number handy. #### 13b. Mosquito-Borne Illness & Insect Protection Mosquito-borne diseases are among the most significant health risks for travelers to tropical destinations. Cover this section clearly. **Key diseases to flag per destination:** | **Disease** | **Mosquito Type** | **Peak Risk** | **Prevention** | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | **Dengue Fever** | Aedes (daytime biting) | Rainy season (May-Oct) but year-round risk | DEET repellent, covered clothing, mosquito nets, staying in air-conditioned rooms. | | **Malaria** | Anopheles (night biting) | Year-round in endemic zones (rural, forested areas) | Anti-malaria medication (if advised), DEET repellent, mosquito nets, covered clothing. | | **Zika Virus** | Aedes | Rainy season | DEET repellent, covered clothing (important for pregnant travelers or those planning conception). | | **Chikungunya** | Aedes | Rainy season | DEET repellent, covered clothing. | **DEET repellent guidance:** - Minimum 30% DEET concentration for effective protection. - Apply to all exposed skin and re-apply every 4-6 hours, or more frequently if sweating heavily or swimming. - Apply sunscreen first, then repellent. - Use permethrin-treated clothing (or spray your own clothes/bed nets) for extended outdoor exposure, especially in rural areas. - Sleep under mosquito nets where air conditioning is unavailable or windows are open. Most guesthouses/hotels in Laos will have them if needed. > **Laos-specific:** DEET-based mosquito repellent is mandatory — not optional. Dengue Fever is a real and present risk year-round in Laos, including in cities like Vientiane and Luang Prabang. Mosquitoes are most active at dawn and dusk, but Aedes mosquitoes (dengue carriers) bite during the day. Apply repellent morning and evening without exception, and reapply as needed. #### 13c. Water & Food Safety Water and food safety rules vary dramatically by destination and must be stated plainly. **Water safety framework:** | **Source** | **Safety** | **Guidance** | |:---|:---|:---| | **Tap water** | Unsafe | In Laos, tap water is completely unsafe to drink. | | **Sealed bottled water** | Safe | Standard recommendation for all consumption. Widely available. | | **Ice in restaurants** | Generally safe in tourist-focused restaurants | Most reputable establishments use commercially produced ice from filtered water. Be cautious at very local street stalls. | | **Filtered water stations** | Safe | Many hotels/guesthouses offer large filtered water dispensers to refill personal bottles — use these! | | **Boiled water** | Safe | Reliable if fully boiled (1 minute at a rolling boil). | > **Laos-specific:** Tap water is completely unsafe throughout Laos. Do not drink it, do not use it to brush teeth unless you are absolutely sure it has been boiled or filtered (e.g., in a hotel room kettle). Rely exclusively on sealed bottled water (widely available, 5,000–10,000 LAK per litre) or use hotel-provided filtered water stations. In restaurants, ice is generally safe in tourist-oriented places, but confirm if you are sensitive. Avoid salads washed in tap water, unpeeled fruits, and raw foods. **Food safety guidance (research per destination):** - **Street food**: Laos has fantastic street food. Eat from busy, high-turnover stalls where food is cooked fresh in front of you and served hot. The high turnover ensures ingredients are fresh. Avoid stalls with food sitting out for long periods. - **Avoid raw salads, unpeeled raw fruit, and raw shellfish** in high-risk destinations. Stick to fruits you can peel yourself (banana, mango, papaya). - **Eat food that is freshly cooked and served hot.** - **Carry oral rehydration sachets** — traveller's diarrhoea is common, and dehydration is the main risk. Rehydration salts (ORS) are available at local pharmacies. - Wash hands frequently with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand sanitiser before eating. #### 13d. Personal Safety & Crime Awareness Honest, specific safety information — neither alarmist nor dismissive. Give travelers the real picture. - **Overall safety rating**: Low to Moderate risk for tourists. Laos is generally a safe country, especially Luang Prabang. However, petty crime does occur, particularly in Vientiane. - **Most common issues**: Petty theft (bag snatching), tuk-tuk/taxi scams (overcharging), drug scams. - **High-risk areas**: Unlit areas at night, deserted streets, crowded markets, and bars/nightclubs where drinks might be spiked. - **Safe areas**: Most tourist zones in Vientiane, Luang Prabang, and Pakse are generally safe during the day. ``` ISSUE: Bag-snatching from motorbikes WHERE IT HAPPENS: Primarily in Vientiane (especially along main roads, riverside area) and less frequently in Luang Prabang. HOW IT HAPPENS: Thieves on passing motorbikes snatch bags, phones, or cameras from pedestrians or from passengers in open tuk-tuks. HOW TO AVOID IT: Keep bags strapped across the body and worn on the side away from the road. Do not hold phones or cameras loosely on busy streets. Be extra vigilant when walking near roads. In a tuk-tuk, keep valuables on the floor between your feet, not on your lap or seat. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Do not resist. Report to tourist police (if available) or local police, then your embassy and insurance company. ISSUE: Tuk-tuk and motorbike taxi scams (overcharging) WHERE IT HAPPENS: Airports, bus stations, popular tourist attractions. HOW IT HAPPENS: Drivers quote inflated prices or change the agreed price upon arrival. HOW TO AVOID IT: Always agree on a price BEFORE boarding. Use ride-hailing apps like LOCA (Vientiane) for transparent pricing. Have small denominations ready to avoid "no change" excuses. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Politely refuse to pay the extra, pay the agreed amount, and walk away. If a large dispute, involve hotel staff. ISSUE: Drug-related scams WHERE IT HAPPENS: Bars (especially in Vang Vieng), guesthouses. HOW IT HAPPENS: You might be offered drugs (marijuana, opium) and then reported to "police" (often fake or corrupt) who demand a large bribe. HOW TO AVOID IT: Laos has very strict drug laws with severe penalties. Do not engage with anyone offering drugs. Do not accept drinks from strangers. Avoid bars known for drug activity. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Do not engage. If approached by "police," try to contact your embassy or a trusted local (hotel staff). ISSUE: Drink Spiking WHERE IT HAPPENS: Bars and nightclubs, particularly in Vang Vieng. HOW IT HAPPENS: Unattended drinks may be spiked, leading to incapacitation and theft. HOW TO AVOID IT: Never leave your drink unattended. Always buy drinks from reputable establishments. Avoid accepting drinks from strangers. Stay with friends. WHAT TO DO IF IT HAPPENS: Seek immediate medical attention. Report to local police and your embassy. ``` #### 13e. SEASONAL CONSIDERATIONS - **Dry Season (October to February)**: * **Weather**: Cool and dry, with clear skies. Temperatures in Vientiane and Luang Prabang range from 15-25°C (59-77°F). Northern mountainous regions can be cooler at night. * **Best for**: Outdoor activities, trekking, sightseeing, comfortable travel. * **What to pack**: Lightweight layers, a light jacket/sweater for evenings, comfortable walking shoes, sun protection. - **Hot Season (March to May)**: * **Weather**: Extremely hot and dry, with temperatures often exceeding 35°C (95°F). Humidity starts to rise towards May. * **Worst for**: Extended outdoor activities. * **What to pack**: Very light, breathable clothing (cotton, linen), wide-brimmed hat, strong sunscreen, hydration salts. Stay hydrated! - **Rainy Season (May to September)**: * **Weather**: Hot and humid, with frequent heavy downpours, typically in the afternoon. Lush green landscapes. Temperatures 25-30°C (77-86°F). * **Considerations**: Roads can be muddy or impassable in rural areas. River travel (e.g., Mekong cruises) can be better due to higher water levels. Mosquitoes are more prevalent. * **What to pack**: Lightweight, quick-drying clothing, waterproof jacket/poncho, insect repellent (DEET mandatory), closed-toe shoes that can get wet. ## 15. MONEY SAVING TIPS - **Tourist discount passes**: Laos doesn't have official "tourist passes" like some other countries. Look for combo tickets if visiting multiple sites at once (e.g., temples in Luang Prabang, though not common). - **Affordable restaurants with good food**: Eat at local street stalls and small family-run restaurants for the best value and authentic food. Look for places busy with locals. Lunch specials are often cheaper. - **Free activities**: * Watching the sunset over the Mekong River (Vientiane) or Nam Khan River (Luang Prabang). * Exploring local markets (morning and night markets). * Visiting some less prominent temples (many don't charge entry). * Walking around the colonial architecture in Luang Prabang. - Participating in informal English conversation practice with monks/students (Luang Prabang, Big Brother Mouse). - **Transportation passes**: No specific urban transport passes. For intercity travel, booking buses/trains at local agencies can sometimes be cheaper than online portals, but less convenient. For tuk-tuks, always negotiate and try to share with others. - **Bargaining**: Always bargain politely in markets and with tuk-tuk drivers. - **Refill water bottles**: Use filtered water stations at hotels/guesthouses to save money and reduce plastic waste. - **Happy Hour**: Look for happy hour specials at bars for cheaper drinks, especially in the early evening. - **Local Beer**: Stick to Beerlao; imported alcohol is significantly more expensive.
